title: Japanese Chicken Curry (Kare Raisu)
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into bite-size pieces
2 large yellow onions (about 1 1/2 lb), cut into thick wedges
1 tsp fresh ginger, grated (with its juice)
2 carrots, peeled and cut into rolling wedges
3 Yukon gold potatoes, peeled and quartered (see notes on russets)
4 cups chicken stock (or half stock half water for less salt)
1/2 apple, peeled and grated - OR 3 Tbsp unsweetened applesauce
1 Tbsp honey (cut to 1 1/2 tsp if using sweetened applesauce)
1 package Japanese curry roux, 7-8 oz (S&B Golden Curry, Vermont Curry, Java Curry)
Steamed Japanese short-grain rice, to serve
Fukujinzuke (red pickled vegetables), to serve - optional
steps: Cut the potatoes and soak them in water 15 min to pull out excess starch. Season the chicken pieces with black pepper.

Heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium. Add the onion wedges and saute about 5 min until translucent - do not stir too often or they will not take on colour. If you have 5 more minutes, give them 5 more; this is where a lot of the flavour comes from.
Add the garlic and grated ginger and stir through.
Add the chicken and cook, stirring, just until no longer pink on the outside. Lower the heat if the onions are browning too hard.
Add the stock, grated apple (or applesauce), honey, soy sauce and ketchup.
Add the carrots and potatoes. The liquid should BARELY cover everything - more than that and the curry comes out thin, and the meat and vegetables will release more as they cook.

Bring to a simmer and skim the foam and scum off the surface. Cover and cook on medium-low about 15 min, stirring now and then, until a skewer goes through the carrots and potatoes. (Simmer uncovered instead if everything is fully submerged.)

TURN OFF THE HEAT. Put 1-2 roux cubes in a ladleful of the hot cooking liquid and let them dissolve completely, stirring with a spoon, then stir that back into the pot. Repeat 2 cubes at a time until the whole package is in.
Turn the heat back to medium-low and simmer UNCOVERED 5-10 min, stirring often and scraping the bottom, until it thickens. Thin with a splash of water if it goes too far.
Serve over short-grain rice, with fukujinzuke on the side if you have it.
notes: APPLESAUCE INSTEAD OF GRATED APPLE: 3 Tbsp unsweetened. Half an apple is about 3 oz of pulp, but applesauce is wetter and already broken down so slightly less goes further. If yours is sweetened, drop the honey to 1 1/2 tsp or skip it - otherwise the curry turns cloying. OTHER SUBS for the apple: grated pear (slightly floral, very good here); 1 Tbsp mango chutney (sweet, fruity and a little acidic - arguably better than apple); 1/4 cup apple juice, subtracted from the stock so you do not thin the sauce; or just bump the honey to 2 Tbsp and accept a bit less body. Avoid plain brown sugar on its own - you get the sweetness with none of the roundness and it ends up tasting flat-sweet. The apple is there for fruit sweetness and a little pectin body, not for any apple flavour you would notice. DISSOLVE THE ROUX IN A LADLE, OFF THE HEAT, two cubes at a time. Dropping the blocks straight into the pot is the classic mistake - they clump, sink, and scorch on the bottom. Heat off, ladle of hot broth, stir until smooth, pour back. BARELY COVER THE SOLIDS with liquid. Japanese curry should coat a spoon, not pour like soup, and you cannot un-thin it later without adding more roux. HEAT LEVEL: a standard box comes mild / medium hot / hot, and Japanese 'hot' lands around a mild-medium for most American palates. Buy Hot if you want any heat at all, and if it is still tame stir in 1/2 tsp cayenne or a spoonful of garam masala at the end. BOX SIZE: a full-size box is 7-8 oz and feeds 8-12. Some brands sell a small 4-serving box - check the weight or you will end up with watery curry. THE APPLE, HONEY, SOY AND KETCHUP are the point, not garnish. That combination is what gives Japanese curry its sweet-savoury backbone; skip them and it tastes like plain roux. POTATOES: Yukon gold holds its shape. Russets fall apart - if that is what you have, cut them into 6 pieces and add them only for the last 15-20 min. SUBS: beef, pork, shrimp, tofu or mushrooms all work. Quick-cooking additions (mushrooms, zucchini, squash) go in for the last 5 min; tofu goes in right after the roux just to warm through. STORING: fridge 3 days, freezer 1 month - but pull the potatoes out before freezing, they go mealy. REHEATING: it sets into a paste in the fridge and will scorch if you reheat it as is. Stir in 1/2 cup of water first, then warm it gently on low. It genuinely tastes better on day two.

title: Arroz Amarillo (Yellow Rice)
source: Cuban/Puerto Rican standard - built on the Salima's Kitchen 30-minute version
ingredients: 1/2 green bell pepper, finely chopped - NO PEPPER? use 1 stalk celery, finely diced
1 packet Sazon con Azafran (Goya, the orange packets) - or 1 tsp turmeric + 1/2 tsp paprika + 1 tsp salt
3 cups broth (chicken or vegetable), or water plus 2 tsp bouillon
Salt - go light, the Sazon and broth are both salty
steps: Rinse the rice in a sieve until the water runs clear, then shake it dry. Skip this and the grains clump.
Heat the oil or butter in a pot with a tight lid over medium. Cook the onion and bell pepper (or celery) 5 min until soft, then the garlic 1 min more.
Add the rice and stir to coat every grain. Toast 1-2 min - this is what keeps it fluffy instead of sticky.
Add the Sazon, cumin, oregano and bay leaf. Stir 30 seconds.
Pour in the broth and stir once. Taste the liquid - it should taste a touch too salty, because the rice will absorb it. Bring to a boil.
Boil uncovered until the liquid drops to the level of the rice and small craters appear across the surface, about 5 min.
Stir once, clamp the lid on, turn the heat to LOW and cook 18-20 min. Do not lift the lid and do not stir.
Take it off the heat, scatter the peas over the top if using, put the lid back on and leave it 10 min. Fish out the bay leaf and fluff with a fork.
notes: NO GREEN PEPPER? USE CELERY - 1 stalk, diced finer than you would for soup (it stays firmer than pepper does). It is vegetal and slightly bitter, which is exactly the job green bell is doing here. Poblano or cubanelle are closer still, and cubanelle is the more traditional Cuban choice anyway; red or orange bell works but runs sweeter. No pepper and no celery at all? Use the whole onion instead of half - you lose a little depth and nothing else. DO NOT ADD CARROT: onion-celery-carrot is a French mirepoix and makes this taste sweet, like a pilaf. Sofrito is onion, pepper, garlic. SAZON IS THE SHORTCUT. One packet of Goya Sazon con Azafran per 2 cups of rice gives you the colour and most of the flavour in one move - it is annatto, coriander, cumin, garlic, MSG and a lot of salt, which is why the added salt here is light. In any supermarket, orange box. NO SAZON? 1 tsp turmeric + 1/2 tsp paprika + 1 tsp salt gets you close on colour and is honestly fine. Bijol powder is the other Cuban standby. Real saffron is a different, more floral dish and costs 20x as much. JARRED SOFRITO (Goya, in the refrigerated section) replaces the onion, pepper and garlic entirely - 2 Tbsp, straight into the hot oil. That is the genuinely lazy version and it is good. NO FRESH AROMATICS AT ALL? 1 1/2 tsp onion powder plus 1/2 tsp garlic powder, but add them WITH the Sazon after the rice is toasted, not at the start - powders scorch in seconds with nothing to sweat. Add a teaspoon of bouillon to the broth and a squeeze of lime at the end to make up the lost depth. THE CRATER CUE beats the clock: when the liquid has fallen to the level of the rice and little holes open across the top, that is the moment to cover and drop the heat. DO NOT LIFT THE LID OR STIR once it is covered. Stirring rice mid-cook knocks starch off the grains and makes it gummy - this is the single most common way yellow rice goes wrong. THE 10-MINUTE REST off the heat matters as much as the cooking; the grains finish on residual steam and firm up. Peas go in during the rest so they warm through without turning grey. RATIO: 1 1/2 cups liquid per cup of rice works for most long-grain. If your bag says 2:1, add another 1/4-1/2 cup. Brown rice will not work with these times. GOES WITH: the slow cooker pork adobo, black beans, roast chicken, anything saucy. Leftovers reheat best with a splash of water, covered, in the microwave.

title: Pork Adobo, Slow Cooker (Boneless)
totalTime: 5-8 hr depending on cut (25 min hands-on) + marinating
servings: 8-10 from a 4-5 lb roast; 6-8 from precut stew meat
source: Adapted for the slow cooker from the Tsingtao oven version (Isabel Lee, Forsyth Fire Escape)
ingredients: 4-5 lb boneless skinless pork shoulder - a whole Boston butt with the fat cap on, OR precut boneless picnic stew meat
1 head garlic, mashed to a paste (or 4 Tbsp jarred minced - see notes)
Juice of 1 lime (about 2 Tbsp), plus wedges to serve
3 Tbsp vegetable oil, melted butter or mayonnaise - or skip it, see notes
3/4 to 1 cup Modelo Especial (3/4 cup for precut, 1 cup for a whole roast)
steps: WHOLE ROAST: pat dry, score the fat cap in a crosshatch about 1/4 inch deep, and cut 1-inch slits all over the meat. PRECUT STEW MEAT: pull off the hard white fat pads and any thick membrane, leaving the marbling and thin fat - no scoring needed.
Mash or blend the garlic to a paste. Mix it with the paprika, onion powder, cumin, oregano, black pepper, salt, lime juice and fat.
Rub the marinade over every surface and down into the slits. Put the pork straight into the slow cooker insert, cover, and refrigerate 4 hours to overnight.
Set the insert into a COLD slow cooker base - never a preheated one, a cold ceramic insert can crack. Whole roast goes fat side up. Pour the beer down the side of the crock, not over the pork.

Cook on LOW until a fork twists with no resistance: 7-8 hours for a whole roast, 5-6 hours for precut chunks. Add about 45 min to either if the insert went in straight from the fridge. It holds on WARM afterwards.

Lift the pork onto a board. Pour the cooking liquid into a tall narrow container, skim or chill off the fat (15-20 min in the freezer sets it into a cap you can lift straight off), then pour it into a saucepan.
Reduce the liquid by about a third, then TASTE before going further - cut pork gives up a saltier liquid than a whole roast, and reducing concentrates it.
Heat the broiler to HIGH/550F with a rack about 6 inches below the element. Shred or pull the pork, discarding any big pockets of fat, and spread it in a single layer on a foil-lined sheet pan.
Spoon about 1/2 cup of the reduced juices over the meat. Broil 5-8 min, checking at 4, until the edges are crisp and browned - watch it, it goes from brown to burnt in under a minute.

Toss the meat, spoon over a little more juice, and broil another 3-5 min for a second round of crispy edges. Lift the meat off the pan with a spatula rather than scraping the rendered fat back in. Serve with the remaining sauce and lime wedges.
notes: THIS IS THE BONELESS, SKINLESS SLOW COOKER VERSION of the Tsingtao oven roast. The original is an 8-10 lb bone-in SKIN-ON shoulder whose whole payoff is crackling from a 450F blast; a slow cooker steams, so skin comes out gray and gelatinous. Without skin that problem disappears and you crisp the SHREDDED meat instead - carnitas style, crunchy edges all the way through instead of one sheet of crackling, and better for tacos. DO NOT SKIP THE BROIL. Slow-cooked pork with no browning step tastes flat and looks grey; those 5-8 minutes are where all the roasted flavor comes from. Rack 6 inches down, not the top slot, or the top chars while the rest stays cold. DEGREASING: lift the meat out first with a slotted spoon, then deal with the liquid alone - chasing fat around shredded pork is hopeless. Tall narrow container, 15-20 min in the freezer, lift the solid cap off. In a hurry: let it settle 5 min, skim with a shallow ladle, then lay flat paper towels on the surface and peel them off, two or three passes. Degrease BEFORE reducing or you concentrate a greasy sauce. The broil is a second degreasing - the fat renders onto the pan. PRECUT STEW MEAT works fine and is often cheaper, but: trim it first (boneless picnic stew runs fatty and sinewy - expect to lose 15-20% to trim), knock 2 hours off the cook, and expect a smaller yield. 4 lb of trays gives roughly 2-2.5 lb of cooked meat. All that cut surface also means the marinade penetrates fully rather than sitting on the outside, so the cooking liquid comes out saltier - taste it before reducing it hard. THE OIL IS NEARLY OPTIONAL. In a slow cooker braise it is not searing anything, it is only helping the spice paste spread, and pork shoulder brings plenty of its own fat. No oil in the house? Melted butter or 3 Tbsp of mayonnaise both work (mayo is mostly oil and clings better than oil does), or leave it out entirely and loosen the paste with a tablespoon of the beer. OVERNIGHT MARINADE IS GOOD, not risky. One lime across 4-5 lb of pork is far too dilute to do any damage in 8-10 hours, and 1 Tbsp of salt over that weight is a dry-brine level that wants the time. Mushy exteriors come from much more acid or 24+ hours. EARLY START: marinate in the slow cooker insert itself the night before, then in the morning just drop the insert into a cold base, add the beer and switch on. ONLY 3/4 TO 1 CUP OF BEER, not the bottle the original calls for. A slow cooker has no evaporation and pork throws off plenty of its own liquid - a full bottle leaves it boiling in a pond instead of steaming above it. Chunks release liquid faster than a roast, hence the smaller amount. BEER: Modelo Especial is a direct swap for Tsingtao, both pale lagers, Modelo slightly maltier. Negra Modelo works too but gives a darker, roastier, more caramel sauce. GARLIC: one head is about 10-12 cloves, roughly 3 Tbsp minced or 1.5 oz by weight. Jarred pre-minced is milder and slightly sour from the citric acid it is packed in, so use 4 Tbsp of it rather than 3. YIELD: plan about 1 lb of raw boneless pork per person for a plated main, less for tacos. Bone-in runs about an hour longer than boneless. SERVE WITH the arroz amarillo in this box. LEFTOVERS shred and freeze well; re-crisp under the broiler rather than microwaving. Good in tacos, on rice, in sandwiches with pickled onion.

title: Tortellini in Frizzled Onion Broth
ingredients: 3 cloves garlic, smashed (add late - see notes)
2 oz shiitake mushroom caps, thinly sliced
4 cups good-quality broth (chicken, beef or vegetable)
Finely grated Parmesan or Pecorino Romano, to serve (optional)
Crusty bread or sourdough croutons, to serve (optional)
steps: Heat a medium pot over medium-high. Add the butter and, once it starts to foam, the olive oil. Swirl to combine.

Add the onion and mushrooms (hold the garlic back - see notes). Season with salt and pepper and cook, stirring often, until the onions are deeply browned, nearly burned, 12-15 min. That colour is the whole dish - do not stop early.
Add the smashed garlic and cook about 1 min, just until fragrant.
Pour in the sherry vinegar to deglaze, scraping up every browned bit off the bottom.
Add the broth (plus 1 cup water if you want it brothier), raise the heat to high and bring to a boil. Taste and season with salt.
Add the tortellini, stir so they do not stick, and cook to the LOW end of the package time - just shy of al dente.
Divide between bowls. Top with chives, Parmesan and more black pepper. Crusty bread or croutons alongside.
notes: FRIZZLED, NOT CARAMELIZED: the point of this recipe is hard and fast, not low and slow - 12-15 min on medium-high until the onions are nearly burnt. That near-burnt edge is the flavour; pulling them at golden gives you a thin, sweet soup instead of an assertive one. GARLIC GOES IN LATE: the recipe says to add it with the onions, but several commenters found it scorches over 15 minutes at that heat and turns bitter. Add it in the last minute before the vinegar instead - the step above is written that way. CRISPY VERSION (from a commenter): fry the onion and mushroom hard for about 5 min until crisp but not softened, lift them out onto paper towels, then build the broth and scatter them back on at serving for texture on top. SALT LATE AND LIGHTLY - about 1,490 mg of sodium a serving as written, and the broth and the tortellini are both already salted. Season at the end, not the start. SUBS: red or white wine vinegar for the sherry vinegar, both commenter-tested. Baby bella or white mushrooms instead of shiitake, cheaper and fine. Any cheese-filled pasta works. A handful of spinach wilted in at the end is a good addition. MAKE AHEAD (the recipe's own tip): the broth keeps 2 days in the fridge WITHOUT the tortellini - bring it back to a boil and cook the pasta right before serving. Do not store leftovers with the tortellini in them; they bloat, go mushy and drink the broth. Cook only as much pasta as you are eating. 2 to 3 servings is small - it doubles without any changes.

title: Rigatoni with Broccoli-Lemon Sauce
ingredients: 1 lb broccoli, stems and florets separated
Kosher salt and ground black pepper
4 Tbsp (1/2 stick) salted butter, cut into 4 pieces
2 Tbsp finely grated lemon zest, divided
1 oz Pecorino Romano or Parmesan, finely grated (1/2 cup), plus more to serve
steps: Bring 4 quarts water and 2 Tbsp salt to a boil in a large pot.

Peel the broccoli stems, reserving any leaves, and cut crosswise into 1/2-inch rounds. Add the stems and leaves to the boiling water and cook until fully tender, about 10 min. Stir in the spinach and cook until wilted, about 20 seconds. Lift the vegetables out with a slotted spoon into a blender, and reserve 1/2 cup of the cooking water. Keep the water at a boil.

Cut the florets into 1- to 1 1/2-inch pieces. Add them to the boiling water and cook until crisp-tender, about 3 min. Lift them out with the slotted spoon into a colander and rinse under cold water until cooled. Keep the water at a boil.

To the blender add the garlic, butter, capers, pepper flakes, 3/4 tsp salt, 1 Tbsp of the lemon zest and the reserved 1/2 cup broccoli cooking water. Puree until smooth and bright green, about 30 seconds. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
Stir the rigatoni into the boiling water and cook until al dente. Reserve 1/2 cup of the cooking water, then drain.

Return the pasta to the pot and add the broccoli florets, the broccoli puree, 1/4 cup of the reserved pasta water, the remaining 1 Tbsp lemon zest and the cheese. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until the sauce thickens slightly and the pasta is well coated, 1-2 min.
Off the heat, taste and season with salt and pepper. Serve with more cheese.
notes: ONE POT OF WATER DOES THREE JOBS - stems, then florets, then the pasta. Do not dump it between steps, and do not skip reserving the 1/2 cup after the broccoli: that starchy, heavily salted water IS the liquid in the sauce, and it is where most of the seasoning comes from. 2 Tbsp of salt in 4 quarts sounds like a lot and is correct. THE STEMS ARE THE SAUCE, not scraps - peel them first, the skin is what makes stems fibrous. Any leaves on the head go in too. THE SPINACH IS FOR COLOR: the stems need a full 10 min to get tender, which is long enough to dull their green, and the spinach wilted in at the end brings the color back. That is why it is in there. RINSE THE FLORETS COLD - it stops the cooking so they stay crisp-tender and bright instead of going olive in the hot pasta. THE BUTTER GOES IN COLD, straight into the blender, and emulsifies with the hot vegetables and starchy water into a creamy sauce with no cream in it. ZEST IS SPLIT ON PURPOSE: 1 Tbsp blended into the sauce for depth, 1 Tbsp at the very end for brightness. Do not put it all in at once. Zest only, no juice - the acid would break the emulsion. 1-2 MINUTES AT THE END, no longer; cooking the finished sauce dulls both the color and the lemon. PECORINO IS SALTIER than Parmesan - taste before adding any salt at the end.

title: White Chicken Chili (Loaded Up)
source: Built on NYT Cooking - Sarah DiGregorio, with depth fixes borrowed from the Cook's Illustrated method
ingredients: 2 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs (bone-in skin-on is better - see notes)
2 jalapenos (one minced for the pot, one reserved raw for the end)
2 (4-oz) cans FIRE-ROASTED green chiles (Hatch if you can find them)
2-3 chipotles in adobo, minced, plus 1 Tbsp of the adobo sauce
2 tsp ground cumin (half up front, half at the end)
1 tsp dried oregano, Mexican if you have it (half up front, half at the end)
2 (14-oz) cans great northern beans, drained and rinsed
3-4 oz cream cheese, or 1/2 cup sour cream (optional, off heat)
Pickled jalapenos and a splash of their brine, sliced scallion, avocado, sour cream, to serve
steps: Pat the thighs dry and season well with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high and brown the chicken hard, 4-5 min a side, in two batches - you are after color, not cooked through. Move to a plate.
Drop to medium and add the butter to the browned bits. Add the onion and a pinch of salt and cook 8 min until soft, scraping the fond up off the bottom as it loosens.

Add the garlic and 1 minced jalapeno, 1 min. Then the fire-roasted green chiles, the minced chipotles and adobo, 1 tsp cumin, the coriander, onion powder, 1/2 tsp oregano and the cayenne. Cook 2 min, stirring, until it smells strong.
Scrape everything into the slow cooker. Add the chicken and any juices on the plate, the stock, salsa verde and beans. Cover and cook on LOW 4-6 hours.

Pull the chicken out and shred it. Scoop out about 1 cup of beans plus 1 cup of the vegetables and liquid, blend smooth, and stir it back in - that is what gives it body. (An immersion blender, 3 or 4 short pulses right in the pot, does the same thing.)
Whisk the miso and soy sauce into a ladleful of the hot broth until smooth, then stir it into the pot. Return the chicken. Add the corn and the remaining 1 tsp cumin and 1/2 tsp oregano. Cook 10 min.

Off the heat: stir in the cream cheese or sour cream if using, then the lime juice, cilantro, and the second jalapeno minced raw with its seeds. Taste for salt - it will probably need more than you expect.
notes: WHY THESE CHANGES: the original is good but tastes thin on day one, because a slow cooker never browns anything, never reduces, and boils the aromatics for 5 hours. Every change here is aimed at that. BROWN THE CHICKEN - the fond in the bottom of the pot is the single biggest thing the original is missing. THIGHS, not breasts: more fat and collagen, they do not dry out over a long cook, and they shred properly. Bone-in skin-on is better still - brown the skin, build everything in that rendered fat, pull the skin off and drop the bones in the cooker for body; debone after shredding. CHILES: swap plain canned green chiles for FIRE-ROASTED (505 Southwestern or Hatch brand; frozen roasted Hatch is best of all). The jarred salsa verde adds tomatillo tang and body cheaply. The chipotles in adobo are the biggest flavor addition - the original has no smoke at all. BODY IS FLAVOR: blending a cup of beans back in is from the Cook's Illustrated version and it matters more than any spice; thin broth reads as bland even when properly seasoned. Masa harina (2 Tbsp slurried into broth) works too and adds toasted corn flavor. UMAMI: white chili has no tomato, no browned crust, no long-cooked collagen, so it has a real savory hole. White miso fills it without darkening the color; soy adds a back-note. Skip tomato paste - it turns the chili pink-orange and its sweetness fights the tomatillo. SPLIT THE SPICES: half the cumin and oregano up front, half in the last 10 min. Cumin's aroma is volatile and 5 hours of slow cooking blows it off. Blooming the second half in a little butter in a small pan first is better still. FINISH RAW: a whole jalapeno with seeds stirred in at the end - late raw chile heat is sharp and bright, stewed chile heat is dull. Same reason the lime and cilantro go in off the heat. SALT HARD. Bland white chili is under-salted far more often than it is under-spiced - but taste first, because the miso, soy, salsa verde and stock all bring salt of their own. Stovetop instead: 4 cups stock, simmer covered on low about 35 min. LEFTOVERS: drain the solids in a colander over a bowl and you have an enchilada/taquito filling plus a sauce; or thin it back out with stock and 2 cans of hominy for a white posole.

title: Cheesy Carrot & Zucchini Orzo
servings: about 4 kid portions (batch cooks and freezes)
ingredients: 450 ml low-salt chicken or vegetable stock (scant 2 cups)
steps: Heat the oil or butter in a pan over medium-high. Add the garlic, grated carrot and grated zucchini and fry 2-3 min, until soft and fragrant.
Add the orzo and the stock. Stir and bring to a boil.
Turn down to medium and cook 10 min, stirring occasionally so it does not catch on the bottom.
When the orzo is soft, take it off the heat and stir through the grated cheddar. Serve.
notes: The recipe is from a UK baby/toddler account - courgette is zucchini, and it is written as a weaning recipe, suitable from 6 months. THE STOCK IS THE POINT: 450 ml to 190 g orzo is a tight ratio on purpose, so the orzo absorbs almost all of it and goes creamy like a risotto rather than being boiled and drained. Stir every couple of minutes - it will stick and scorch if you walk away. If it tightens up before the orzo is soft, splash in a little more stock or water. CHEESE OFF THE HEAT, always - cheddar stirred into a boiling pan goes stringy and oily. LOW-SALT STOCK matters if a baby or toddler is eating it; regular stock is far too salty for them. For adults it will taste underseasoned - salt and pepper your own bowl at the table rather than the pan. STORING (her numbers): fridge up to 4 days, freezer up to 3 months. It thickens hard as it cools, so loosen with a splash of water or stock when reheating. Grate the veg finely, not coarsely - fine grating is what makes it disappear into the sauce, which is the whole trick with kids.

title: Game Day Pretzel Bites
ingredients: Coarse salt (pretzel salt or coarse kosher)
steps: Heat the oven to 425F and line a sheet pan with parchment.
Cut each biscuit into 6 pieces - 48 bites total.
Bring the water to a boil in a wide pot, then add the baking soda SLOWLY - it foams up hard the second it hits boiling water.
Drop the biscuit pieces into the bath for 20-30 seconds, working in batches so they are not crowded. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and set them on the parchment.
Brush each bite with melted butter and sprinkle with coarse salt.
Bake 12-15 min, until deep golden brown.
notes: THE BAKING SODA BATH IS THE WHOLE TRICK - do not skip it. The alkaline water is what browns the outside and gives you actual pretzel flavor and chew; without it these are just baked biscuit pieces. Add the baking soda to the boiling water a spoonful at a time or it will foam over the pot. 20-30 seconds is enough; leave them longer and they get soapy and slick. WHAT A COMMENTER REPORTED: plain was about a 6/10, but tossed in garlic and parmesan before baking plus more melted butter after the bake it was a 12; a cinnamon sugar version was a 10. Worth doing half the batch savory and half sweet. Brushing again with butter right out of the oven is not in the original but it is what makes them taste like mall pretzels. SERVE: warm, with nacho/beer cheese sauce or grainy mustard. They go soft and tough within an hour or two, so time them to come out when people are ready to eat. 8-count biscuits cut in 6 gives 48 small bites; cut in 4 for bigger ones and add a minute or two in the oven.

title: Senate Bean Soup (Fast, Canned Beans)
source: NYT Cooking - Sarah DiGregorio (the recipe's own faster-version tip)
ingredients: 1 red or yellow onion, finely chopped
3 medium carrots, peeled and sliced 1/2 to 1 inch thick
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, Diamond Crystal (half the original Tbsp - see notes)
8 cups chicken broth (in place of the water)
4 (15-oz) cans navy beans, drained and rinsed
About 1 lb chopped ham (in place of the ham hocks)
1 medium russet potato, peeled and quartered
OPTIONAL: 8 oz kale, stems removed and chopped
steps: Melt the butter in a large soup pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring often, 5-6 min until softened.
Add the garlic and carrots and cook, stirring, about 2 min until the garlic is fragrant and softened.
Add the salt, smoked paprika, thyme and several generous grinds of black pepper. Stir to combine.
Add the broth, drained beans, chopped ham and potato. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a low simmer, cover, and simmer 20-30 min - until the potato is tender and the soup has come together.
Add the kale, if using, in the last 5 min.
Mash the potato pieces against the side of the pot with a fork. Stir vigorously to break down some of the beans too - that is what thickens it.
Stir in the cider vinegar. Taste and add salt and pepper as needed.
notes: This is the recipe's own TIP for a faster version, not a workaround: four 15-oz cans of navy beans for the dried, chopped ham for the ham hocks, chicken broth for the water, salt cut in half, and a 20-30 min simmer instead of the hour-plus. SALT: the original calls for 1 Tbsp kosher salt (Diamond Crystal) with plain water and unsalted dried beans; the tip says halve it, so 1 1/2 tsp. Even that can run high once you factor in salted broth, canned beans and ham - if you are using regular (not low-sodium) broth, start at 1 tsp and season at the end. If you use Morton kosher or table salt, cut it further; Diamond Crystal is much less salty by volume. RINSE THE BEANS - the canning liquid is starchy and salty. THICKENING: canned beans do not release starch the way a long simmer does, so the potato mash and crushing some of the beans matters more here than in the original. Still thin? Mash more beans or simmer a few minutes uncovered. The vinegar at the end is not optional - it is what keeps it from tasting flat. The full 1 hr 45 min version with dried navy beans and two smoked ham hocks is at the link.

title: Cheesy Broccoli, Butternut Squash & Lentils
servings: about 6 kid portions (batch cooks and freezes)
ingredients: 600 ml low-salt chicken or vegetable stock (about 2 1/2 cups)
1 cup butternut squash, peeled and finely grated (or diced very small)
1 cup broccoli florets, chopped very fine (pea-sized)
steps: Rinse the lentils and pick out any small stones or shriveled lentils.
Heat the oil or butter in a pot over medium. Add the garlic and squash and saute 3-4 min, until the squash softens and the garlic is fragrant.
Add the lentils and all the stock. Bring to a boil, then simmer 18-20 min.
Add the broccoli and simmer 8-10 min more, stirring now and then, until the lentils and broccoli are very soft (25-30 min total for the lentils). Add a splash of water if it dries out.
Take it off the heat, mash a little with a fork, and stir in the cheddar.
notes: Lentils-only variation of the Cheesy Carrot & Zucchini Orzo, with brown lentils in place of the orzo, plus broccoli and butternut squash. Make sure the lentils, broccoli and squash are all fork-mashable soft for a toddler; mash more for a smoother texture. Don't add salt: the cheese and low-salt stock are enough for under-2s. Lentils are high in fiber, so start with smaller portions. Cheese goes in off the heat. Pre-cut squash saves the peeling. The squash is sauteed first for flavor and melts into the lentils; the broccoli goes in last so it stays green and doesn't turn sulfury or mushy. Freeze single portions in ice-cube trays and reheat with a splash of water.
